abstract: DeepMind Institute essay by Julian Jacobs and Alex Imas evaluating eleven policies for managing AGI-driven economic disruption. It argues against picking a single prescription and for sequencing policies against observable empirical triggers, since the scenario that will actually materialise cannot be known in advance. A companion paper carries the full methodology and an evaluation of fourteen funding mechanisms.
keyFindings: Three least-regret interventions matched to scenarios: expanded unemployment insurance, EITC and employer-led retraining as preemptive stabilisers for mild disruption; EITC transitioning into a Negative Income Tax if data shows prolonged unemployment spells and falling median wages outpacing job reinstatement; and a Universal Basic Capital backstop triggered if labor's share of GDP declines persistently alongside rising capital returns.

The authors argue against UBI as the default answer: it risks inflationary pressure, is an expensive and blunt instrument, and leaves people with no direct stake in the automated part of the economy. A Negative Income Tax is judged more efficient because it pays only below an income threshold and does not require adjudicating whether a given job loss was caused by AI rather than ordinary churn.

Policy ratings diverge sharply by dimension, which is the essay's main analytical payoff. EITC scores highest on feasibility (79.8) but near the bottom on durability under full AGI transformation (31.9). Universal Basic Capital is the reverse: top of the agency ranking (76.3) and highest single durability score under transformation (93.5), but lowest tier on feasibility (33.1). Active Labour Market Policies score lowest on durability (23.0).

Real US public-opinion findings reported alongside the simulated ratings: 85 percent of Americans support publicly funded worker retraining, 72 percent support unemployment insurance, and 54 percent support a universal basic capital program.

The essay names the measurement problem directly: platform usage metrics cannot reveal net employment effects, workplace field experiments rarely generalise to the macroeconomy, and administrative datasets lag real disruption - so trigger-based policy requires data infrastructure that does not yet exist.
methodology: Manual literature review and surveys combined with an agent-based expert panel: 51 AI agent personas whose attitudes were designed from survey data on 51 real economists, deliberating and rating each policy 0-100 across sub-criteria, using the EDSL approach pioneered by John Horton. Ratings are aggregated into composite scores for welfare and resilience, agency and empowerment, feasibility and implementation, and durability across three AGI scenarios.
qualifiers: The headline scores are not expert opinion in the ordinary sense. They come from simulated economist personas, not from economists - the tables label them 'N = 51 simulated economist personas' and anyone quoting them as an expert panel is overstating them. The authors call the approach exploratory and say experiments and empirical evaluation are needed to validate the policy options. The essay contains no original measurement of AI's labor market effects, which is why jobsdata.ai carries it as a policy and framework source rather than as evidence on any prediction graph. Published 2026-07-09 and updated 2026-09-16. Google DeepMind has a commercial interest in AGI policy framing.
